mcqs.question: New joiners keep getting stuck partway through setting up your service locally. Which README addition most reliably fixes that whole class of problem?
options: A Troubleshooting section listing the three failures newcomers actually hit, quoting the literal error text
A longer Architecture section explaining the event-sourcing model the service is built on
An auto-generated index of every class and public method in the codebase
A link to the team's archive of past design docs
mcqs.explanation: A stuck reader searches for the error string in front of them, so a section containing that exact string is the fastest path from stuck to unstuck — and the three recurring failures are already known to the team. Expanding the architecture section is the tempting alternative because it feels more substantial, but someone whose containers won't start does not have a mental-model problem.

mcqs.question: Your refunds endpoint already publishes an auto-generated table of parameter names, types and required flags. Which addition gives callers something a generator fundamentally cannot?
options: A prose restatement of which fields are required and what type each one is
Example request and response bodies showing the same fields populated
The server-side struct definitions the handler unmarshals the body into

That a 409 charge_already_refunded is safe to treat as success while a 422 charge_too_old is terminal, and that reusing an Idempotency-Key returns the original refund rather than creating a second one
mcqs.explanation: Retry safety, terminal versus retryable errors, and idempotency semantics live in the implementation's behaviour, not in its schema, so no generator can infer them — and they are precisely what a caller otherwise learns during an incident. Worked examples are the most tempting near-miss: genuinely useful, but mechanically derivable from the schema and silent about what happens when the call fails.

mcqs.question: A runbook for a P2 alert has not been executed by anyone in 18 months, though its text has been tidied since. What is the accurate assessment?
options: It is strictly better than nothing, because some guidance always beats none
It is fine, because its "last updated" date is recent
It can be worse than nothing — the on-call engineer trusts it and spends the first 15 minutes of the incident debugging the runbook rather than the outage
It is only a risk if the service itself has been rewritten in that time
mcqs.explanation: Confidently wrong instructions cost more than absent ones, because an absent runbook sends the responder straight to a human while a stale one sends them down failing commands during the worst possible fifteen minutes. A recent edit date proves nothing about whether a namespace was renamed or a flag deprecated — only a "last tested" date, earned by actually running it, does.

mcqs.question: Your team maintains the orders-api runbook both as markdown in the repo and as a Confluence page. Why is keeping both specifically worse than choosing one?
options: Two half-maintained copies means readers hit the stale one roughly half the time; one authoritative home plus a one-line pointer from the other place is strictly better
Confluence cannot render fenced code blocks, so the commands become unusable
Runbooks always belong in a wiki, because non-engineers need to be able to read them
Keeping operational documentation in a source repository violates most access-control policies
mcqs.explanation: Duplication does not double coverage, it halves trust — a reader has no way to tell which copy was updated last, so both become unreliable. The location choice itself is real but decided differently: docs that break when the code changes belong beside the code, while process and org-facing pages belong in the wiki, and neither format is technically incapable of the other's job.

mcqs.question: Which header line tells a paged engineer the most about how far to trust a runbook at 2am?
options: Author: dan@
Last updated: 2026-07-02
Last reviewed: 2026-06-18 by dan@ — a human confirmed these steps still work
Version: 3
mcqs.explanation: "Reviewed" is a claim that someone checked the content against reality, which is exactly the question the reader has. "Last updated" is the tempting substitute and it is much weaker — fixing a typo or reformatting a heading refreshes that date while proving nothing about whether the kubectl commands still resolve.
